report.headline: clickhousectl shows genuine, day-to-day AI-native development — rich agent guidance, heavy AI-assisted commit activity, and a substantial test suite — but the mechanisms that would let that trust scale safely (enforced branch protection, AI-in-CI governance, supply-chain scanning) are still mostly habit rather than codified policy.

Nearly half of recent PRs involve AI assistance (Claude, Cursor) with visible co-author trailers, and every sampled merged PR carried at least one human review.
A large, purpose-built test suite (36 files, 0.78 test-to-source ratio) including an E2E harness that provisions and tears down real ClickHouse Cloud + AWS resources.
Strong supply-chain hygiene where it exists: all third-party Actions pinned by SHA, releases signed with provenance.

Documentation outside the README (CHANGELOG, ADRs, CONTRIBUTING) is largely absent, so the reasoning behind key decisions may only live in commit history or chat logs.
The E2E tests require live cloud/AWS credentials and are excluded from routine runs (#[ignore]), so everyday CI confidence rests on a narrower slice of the suite than the file count suggests.

Infrastructure-as-code is present by definition since the entire repo is Terraform modules, but there's no deploy/apply pipeline (expected for a consumed module), no release/versioning automation, no policy-as-code gate, and no drift detection layered on top of the linting.
strengths: PR-triggered CI with two dedicated validation jobs
Required status checks before merge, backed by branch protection

No release automation, tagging, or changelog for module consumers to pin against

No drift detection or scheduled validation of live infrastructure state

dimensions.name: Documentation & Knowledge
dimensions.summary: Documentation is limited to a 242-character README pointing to the gcp/ and azure/ module folders — there is no /docs directory, no ADRs, no CHANGELOG, and no CONTRIBUTING.md. This is a notable gap given that recent commits carry real security reasoning (dropping User.Invite.All, scoping Graph API permissions, adding NSG rules) that currently exists only in PR titles and descriptions rather than in the repo itself.

gaps: No CHANGELOG.md or CONTRIBUTING.md
No ADRs recording why specific permission scopes were added or removed
No per-module documentation of inputs/outputs or the exact permission set each module grants
Nothing written for an agent to consume before modifying IAM-sensitive HCL

Terraform fmt-check acts as a formatting guardrail, but there's no pre-commit hook config, no commitlint enforcement (only 47% of commits happen to follow convention organically), and no PR template.

Pull requests required to merge (1 approval(s) + code owners)
strengths: CODEOWNERS covering the whole repo with two named teams
Required approval + code-owner review enforced via branch protection

No commitlint/conventional-commit enforcement — adherence is organic (47%), not gated
No PR template found

dimensions.name: Commit & Velocity Signals
dimensions.summary: Thirty recent commits show active, well-paced delivery — median 0.8h to merge and to first review, 93% small PRs — alongside direct evidence of AI-assisted work (one bot-attributed commit, and Claude and Cursor each named in a PR, 7% AI involvement across 27 PRs). Conventional-commit prefixes appear in roughly half of commits. This is meaningfully more AI fingerprint than most infra repos show, even if still early and individual.

dimensions.name: AI Process & Harness
dimensions.summary: No dedicated AI process or harness exists — no evals or golden tests for AI-authored output, no prompt or agent library, no agent-facing runbooks, and no Definition-of-Done connecting AI contributions to review gates. The only structural control visible here is that the default branch carries 2 protection rules, which is a general governance backstop rather than anything specific to AI process.

dimensions.name: Supply Chain & Security
dimensions.summary: Security posture is fixed at 34/100 by the deterministic battery: branch protection is strong (9/10 — protected, 1 approval, status checks, code-owner review) and no dangerous workflow patterns exist (10/10 — no script-injection or untrusted-checkout patterns), but every supply-chain control scores 0/10 — no explicit `permissions:` scope on the single workflow, no SAST/IaC scanning, no dependency-update bot, 0 of 4 action references pinned by SHA, no SECURITY.md, and no signed releases or SBOM. Because this repo's entire content is Terraform that grants and scopes customer cloud IAM/Graph permissions, the absence of IaC-aware security scanning and pinned/updated Actions is a higher-stakes gap than it would be in a typical application repo.
evidence: Branch protection [posture/high]: 9/10 — Default branch: protected, 1 approval(s), status checks, code-owner review.
Dangerous workflow [posture/critical]: 10/10 — No script-injection or untrusted-checkout patterns detected.
Token permissions [posture/high]: 0/10 — 0/1 workflows set an explicit `permissions:` scope.
SAST [posture/medium]: 0/10 — No SAST (CodeQL/Semgrep/Sonar) wired into CI.
Dependency updates [posture/high]: 0/10 — No dependency-update tool committed.
Pinned dependencies [posture/medium]: 0/10 — 0/4 Actions/images pinned by SHA/digest (4 action refs).
Security policy [posture/medium]: 0/10 — No security policy (SECURITY.md) found.
Signed releases [posture/high]: 0/10 — No artifact signing / provenance in CI.
Known vulnerabilities [exposure/high]: n/a/10 — Dependency vulnerabilities not inspected (no lockfile / no alert access).
strengths: Strong branch protection: required approval, status checks, and code-owner review all enforced
No dangerous workflow patterns (script injection, untrusted checkout) detected in CI
gaps: Add a least-privilege top-level `permissions:` block (default `contents: read`) to every workflow.
Add CodeQL (or Semgrep) scanning that runs on pull_request.
Add a `.github/dependabot.yml` (or Renovate) config.
Pin third-party Actions to a full commit SHA (and container images to a digest).
Add a SECURITY.md describing how to report vulnerabilities.
Sign releases with cosign and emit SLSA provenance (actions/attest).
Generate an SBOM (Syft/CycloneDX) on release.

report.headline: A disciplined, fast-moving infrastructure team runs a security-sensitive IAM Terraform repo largely by hand: human review is fast and clean (100% reviewed, 0% reverted, 0.8h median merge), but AI usage so far is individual and unconventioned, with no tests, no agentic workflows, and no IaC-aware supply-chain hardening around the permission grants this repo actually ships.
strengths: Fast, disciplined human review culture: 100% of merged PRs reviewed, 0% reverted, median 0.8h to merge and to first review, 93% small PRs
Branch protection and CODEOWNERS enforce a real gate (1 approval + code-owner review) on every change to IAM-granting Terraform
Individual engineers are already reaching for Claude and Cursor in real commits/PRs — a seed of AI adoption worth formalizing
CI runs terraform validate and fmt-check on every PR, and the repo is infrastructure-as-code end-to-end by design
risks: Zero automated tests for Terraform modules that grant/revoke cloud IAM and Graph API permissions — correctness relies entirely on human eyes

No IaC-aware security scanning (tfsec/checkov) or dependency-update automation, combined with 0/4 unpinned GitHub Actions — a real supply-chain gap for a repo whose blast radius is customer cloud-permission grants
No shared AI guidance (CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md) leaves the AI usage already happening (Claude, Cursor) unmoored from any team convention or test discipline
Minimal documentation (242-character README, no ADRs) leaves no recorded rationale for why specific permission scopes were added or removed
No AI-in-process harness (no evals, no agent runbooks) — nothing yet makes AI contributions repeatable or independently verifiable

roadmap.title: Individual engineers already reach for AI tools here, but nothing shared guides them
roadmap.rationale: Claude and Cursor already appear in this repo's commit/PR history, but without a CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md the team has no shared record of validate/fmt/plan commands, the permission model each module encodes, or where AI assistance should tread carefully given the IAM blast radius.
explore: What would it look like to write down, once, the terraform validate/fmt/plan commands and the permission model each module encodes, so any agent or new engineer starts from the same page?
Are there constraints around IAM/Graph-permission changes the team already applies informally in review that would be worth making explicit for an agent?
Which habits from the engineers already using Claude/Cursor here would be most useful to capture for the rest of the team?

roadmap.title: Permission-granting Terraform changes merge on human review alone, with no automated check behind it
roadmap.rationale: Recent history shows commits scoping down Graph API permissions, adding NSG rules, and creating custom roles — high-blast-radius changes — yet the only CI check is syntax validation and formatting; nothing verifies the resulting permission set matches intent before a reviewer has to catch it by eye.
explore: What would a lightweight test (Terratest, or a policy check against expected IAM scopes) look like for the highest-risk module here?
Is there a way to encode 'this role should never have X permission' as a check, given how often permission scoping shows up in this repo's history?
Would the team find value in trying checkov or tfsec as a fast way to get baseline IaC security feedback before investing in deeper tests?

roadmap.title: The repo grants cloud IAM permissions but has no IaC security scanning or dependency-update automation watching it
roadmap.rationale: Branch protection and workflow safety are strong (9/10, 10/10), but SAST/IaC scanning, dependency-update bots, pinned Actions, and a security policy are all absent — for a repo whose entire content is customer cloud-permission grants, that's a wider gap between what's protected and what's automatically checked than the branch-protection score alone suggests.
explore: Would it be worth trying tfsec or checkov against these modules to see what it surfaces, given how often permission scopes change here?
Is there an appetite for Dependabot/Renovate to keep the two third-party GitHub Actions in lint.yaml current, and pin them by SHA?
Does a SECURITY.md or documented disclosure path make sense for a module that customers' cloud accounts depend on?

roadmap.title: Early AI usage isn't yet supported by any process that would make it repeatable or reviewable as such
roadmap.rationale: With AI already touching about 7% of PRs but no evals, prompt library, or agent runbooks, there's no way yet to tell whether AI-assisted changes to this IAM-sensitive codebase get a different — or equally rigorous — review path than human-authored ones.
explore: Would it help to know, going forward, which PRs had AI involvement, so the team can see whether review depth differs?
Is there a small, recurring type of change here (e.g. permission scoping) that would benefit from a documented runbook an agent could follow consistently?

roadmap.title: The reasoning behind IAM permission changes lives only in PR history, not in the repo itself
roadmap.rationale: The README is two sentences and there are no ADRs or per-module docs — commits like 'drop User.Invite.All' or 'scope provisioner Graph permission' carry real security reasoning that currently only exists in merged PR history, making it harder for a future agent or engineer to reconstruct why a permission boundary sits where it does.
explore: Would a short ADR per significant permission change (why scoped down, why added) be worth trying, given how often that reasoning already appears in PR titles?
Could each module folder (gcp/, azure/) carry a short doc of what it grants and why, as a starting point for both new engineers and agents?
